1 Corinthians 1.audience: Paul writes from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8) around AD 54–55 to the church he founded in Corinth (Acts 18), after reports from "them which are of the house of Chloe" (1 Corinthians 1:11).

culture.title: Corinth
culture.text: Corinth was destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC. By Paul's time it was the capital of Achaia and a busy port city between two harbors.

culture.title: Following teachers
culture.text: Students in Greek cities attached themselves to famous teachers and speakers and boasted of them.

culture.title: Greeks seek after wisdom
culture.text: Crucifixion was a shameful death for slaves and rebels. Greek culture prized philosophy and skilled public speaking.

1 Corinthians 2.audience: Paul reminds the Corinthians that he came to them "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling" (1 Corinthians 2:3).

culture.title: Excellency of speech
culture.text: Traveling orators (sophists) gave paid public displays of eloquence, and audiences judged them by style.

culture.title: Eye hath not seen
culture.text: Paul introduces this with "as it is written"; the wording is close to Isaiah 64:4.

1 Corinthians 3.audience: Paul addresses the Corinthian divisions over Paul and Apollos, using images of farming and building.

culture.title: Milk and meat
culture.text: Teachers in Paul's time compared basic instruction to milk for infants.

culture.title: Building materials
culture.text: Gold, silver, and costly stones survive fire; wood, hay, and stubble burn. Fires were a constant danger in ancient cities.

culture.title: Ye are the temple
culture.text: Corinth had many temples, including the temple of Apollo whose columns still stand.

1 Corinthians 4.audience: Paul says he is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways (1 Corinthians 4:17) and asks whether he should come "with a rod, or in love."

culture.title: Stewards
culture.text: A steward was often a trusted slave who managed a household's business for the owner.

culture.title: Last in the procession
culture.text: In a Roman triumph, captives condemned to death marched at the end of the procession.

culture.title: Instructors and fathers
culture.text: The word for instructor (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a boy on the way to school.

1 Corinthians 5.audience: Paul deals with a man living with his father's wife. He mentions an earlier letter he had written to them (1 Corinthians 5:9).

culture.title: His father's wife
culture.text: The law forbade marrying a stepmother (Leviticus 18:8), and Roman law forbade it as well.

culture.title: Purging out the leaven
culture.text: Before Passover, Jewish households removed all leaven from the house (Exodus 12:15).

1 Corinthians 6.audience: Paul addresses believers taking each other to court and visiting prostitutes.

culture.title: Going to law
culture.text: Roman civil courts favored the wealthy and well-connected. Lawsuits were a common way to compete for status.

culture.title: Meats for the belly
culture.text: Many translations put "All things are lawful unto me" (1 Corinthians 6:12) and "Meats for the belly" in quotation marks, as sayings Paul is answering.

culture.title: Bought with a price
culture.text: Slaves were bought and sold in the market or freed by paying a price.

1 Corinthians 7.audience: Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him: "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me" (1 Corinthians 7:1).

culture.title: The present distress
culture.text: Paul does not say what the distress was. Famines struck parts of the empire in the late 40s and 50s.

culture.title: Called being a servant
culture.text: Roman masters often freed slaves, and a slave freed by a Roman citizen could become a citizen.

culture.title: Married to an unbeliever
culture.text: Plutarch advised that a wife should worship only her husband's gods, so mixed households could face strain.

1 Corinthians 8.audience: Paul answers the Corinthians' question about "things offered unto idols" (1 Corinthians 8:1).

culture.title: Meat offered to idols
culture.text: Animals sacrificed in temples were partly burned, partly eaten by worshipers, and partly sold in the market.

culture.title: Eating in the idol's temple
culture.text: Temples had dining rooms rented for banquets and celebrations. Rooms like these have been excavated at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth.

culture.title: Gods many, and lords many
culture.text: Corinth had temples to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius, Demeter, and the imperial family.

1 Corinthians 9.audience: Paul explains why he did not accept payment from the Corinthians and uses athletic images familiar to the city.

culture.title: Muzzling the ox
culture.text: Oxen treading grain were allowed to eat as they worked (Deuteronomy 25:4).

culture.title: Working with his hands
culture.text: Philosophers were paid by patrons, charged fees, or begged. Paul worked as a tentmaker in Corinth (Acts 18:3).

culture.title: The Isthmian Games
culture.text: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years. Winners received a crown made of pine or withered celery.

1 Corinthians 10.audience: Paul uses Israel's wilderness history as a warning and returns to the question of idol food.

culture.title: Our fathers
culture.text: Paul recalls the cloud, the sea, the manna, and the water from the rock (Exodus 13–17; Numbers 20).

culture.title: The shambles
culture.text: The shambles was the meat market. An inscription from Corinth's market area mentions a macellum.

culture.title: The cup of devils
culture.text: Pagan banquets included a cup of wine poured out as an offering to a god.

1 Corinthians 11.audience: Paul addresses head coverings in worship and disorder at the Lord's supper, where some ate while others went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:21).

culture.title: Head coverings
culture.text: Roman married women covered their heads in public as a sign of modesty. Roman men also covered their heads when offering sacrifice.

culture.title: Dining in homes
culture.text: Roman writers such as Pliny describe hosts serving better food and wine to favored guests than to others at the same meal.

culture.title: The Lord's supper
culture.text: This is the earliest written account of the supper, which Paul says he "received of the Lord" and passed on.

1 Corinthians 12.audience: Paul begins three chapters on spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12–14), reminding them that they "were Gentiles" carried away to dumb idols (1 Corinthians 12:2).

culture.title: Ecstatic worship
culture.text: Some Greek cults, such as that of Dionysus, practiced frenzied worship and inspired speech.

culture.title: The body
culture.text: Clay models of body parts offered for healing have been found at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth. Roman writers also compared society to a body.

1 Corinthians 13.audience: Placed between Paul's two chapters on spiritual gifts, this chapter describes love.

culture.title: Sounding brass
culture.text: Corinth was famous for its bronze. Gongs and cymbals were used in pagan worship.

culture.title: Through a glass, darkly
culture.text: Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect reflection.

culture.title: When I was a child
culture.text: A Roman boy put on the adult toga, the toga virilis, at around fifteen or sixteen.

1 Corinthians 14.audience: Paul gives instructions for tongues and prophecy in the gathered church so that "all things be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40).

culture.title: Musical instruments
culture.text: The pipe (aulos), harp, and trumpet were common instruments; the trumpet signaled soldiers to battle.

culture.title: Barbarian
culture.text: Someone speaking a language the hearer did not understand was called a barbarian.

culture.title: With men of other tongues
culture.text: Paul quotes Isaiah 28:11–12 and calls it "the law."

1 Corinthians 15.audience: Some in Corinth were saying "there is no resurrection of the dead" (1 Corinthians 15:12). Paul lists those to whom the risen Jesus appeared.

culture.title: Received and delivered
culture.text: "Received" and "delivered" were terms Jewish teachers used for passing on tradition.

culture.title: Greek views of the afterlife
culture.text: Many Greeks believed in the soul's survival but thought bodily resurrection impossible (Acts 17:32).

culture.title: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus
culture.text: Criminals were sometimes sent to fight wild animals in the arena. Paul does not explain whether he means this literally.

1 Corinthians 16.audience: Paul gives instructions for the collection, plans to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, and sends greetings. He adds a final greeting in his own hand (1 Corinthians 16:21).

culture.title: Laying by in store
culture.text: Paul asks each believer to set money aside on the first day of the week for the Jerusalem collection.

culture.title: A great door
culture.text: Paul says "a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries." Acts 19 describes his time in Ephesus.

culture.title: Maranatha
culture.text: Maranatha is Aramaic, meaning ‘Our Lord, come’ or ‘Our Lord has come.’

2 Corinthians 1.audience: Paul writes from Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:5) around AD 55–56, explaining why he changed his travel plans.

culture.title: Trouble in Asia
culture.text: Paul says he "despaired even of life" in Asia but gives no details.

culture.title: The earnest of the Spirit
culture.text: An earnest (arrabon) was a first payment or deposit that guaranteed the rest.

2 Corinthians 2.audience: Paul refers to a painful earlier letter written "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4) and asks the church to forgive a man they had punished.

culture.title: Triumph
culture.text: In a Roman triumph, a victorious general led his army and captives through the city. Incense was burned along the route.

culture.title: Corrupting the word
culture.text: The Greek word for ‘corrupt’ was used for peddlers who watered down wine to sell it.

2 Corinthians 3.audience: Paul contrasts the ministry of the new covenant with the law written on stone, recalling Moses' veiled face (Exodus 34:29–35).

culture.title: Letters of commendation
culture.text: Travelers carried letters introducing them to hosts in other cities (Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1).

culture.title: Tables of stone
culture.text: The commandments were written on two stone tablets (Exodus 31:18). Jeremiah 31:33 speaks of the law written in the heart.

culture.title: Moses' veil
culture.text: Moses put a veil over his shining face after speaking with God (Exodus 34:33–35).

2 Corinthians 4.audience: Paul writes about his suffering in ministry: "troubled on every side, yet not distressed" (2 Corinthians 4:8).

culture.title: Earthen vessels
culture.text: Cheap clay jars were used to store everything, including valuables. Clay lamps were also made in Corinth in great numbers.

culture.title: The god of this world
culture.text: Jewish writings of the period describe Satan as ruler over the present age (compare John 12:31).

2 Corinthians 5.audience: Paul describes the earthly body as a tent and calls believers "ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:20).

culture.title: Our earthly house
culture.text: Paul, a tentmaker, compares the body to a tent—a temporary dwelling.

culture.title: The judgment seat
culture.text: The bema in Corinth's forum, where Paul stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12), has been excavated.

culture.title: Ambassadors
culture.text: An ambassador spoke on behalf of a ruler. In the Greek East the word was used for the emperor's representatives.

2 Corinthians 6.audience: Paul lists his hardships and urges the Corinthians to open their hearts to him and separate from idolatry.

culture.title: Unequally yoked
culture.text: The law forbade plowing with an ox and an ass together (Deuteronomy 22:10).

culture.title: Belial
culture.text: Belial means ‘worthlessness.’ In Jewish writings like the Dead Sea Scrolls it is a name for Satan.

culture.title: A chain of Scripture
culture.text: Paul combines Leviticus 26:12, Isaiah 52:11, and 2 Samuel 7:14.

2 Corinthians 7.audience: Titus has brought Paul good news from Corinth while he was in Macedonia (2 Corinthians 7:6–7).

culture.title: Waiting for news
culture.text: Letters and news traveled only as fast as messengers on foot or by ship.

culture.title: Godly sorrow
culture.text: Paul contrasts "godly sorrow" that leads to repentance with "the sorrow of the world."

2 Corinthians 8.audience: Paul encourages the Corinthians to finish the collection for Jerusalem, pointing to the generosity of the Macedonian churches.

culture.title: Deep poverty
culture.text: Paul says the Macedonian churches gave in "a great trial of affliction" and out of "deep poverty" (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:6).

culture.title: Gathering manna
culture.text: Paul quotes Exodus 16:18: "He that had gathered much had nothing over."

culture.title: Handling money honestly
culture.text: Paul sends trusted men with the collection so no one can accuse him of misusing it.

2 Corinthians 9.audience: Paul asks Corinth to have its gift ready before the Macedonians arrive with him.

culture.title: Sowing and reaping
culture.text: Paul uses a farming proverb similar to Proverbs 11:24–25.

culture.title: A cheerful giver
culture.text: The wording echoes Proverbs 22:8 in the Greek Old Testament.

2 Corinthians 10.audience: Paul answers those who say "his letters ... are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak" (2 Corinthians 10:10).

culture.title: Strongholds
culture.text: Paul uses siege language: pulling down fortifications and taking prisoners.

culture.title: Commending themselves
culture.text: Public speakers often praised themselves and compared themselves favorably with rivals.

2 Corinthians 11.audience: Paul reluctantly compares himself with rivals he calls "the very chiefest apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5) and lists his sufferings.

culture.title: A chaste virgin
culture.text: A father pledged his daughter in marriage and guarded her until the wedding.

culture.title: Forty stripes save one
culture.text: Synagogues gave thirty-nine lashes to stay within the limit of forty in Deuteronomy 25:3. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment (Acts 16:22).

culture.title: Aretas
culture.text: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose capital was Petra; he died about AD 40.

2 Corinthians 12.audience: Paul tells of a vision "fourteen years ago" and of a "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:2, 7). He plans a third visit (2 Corinthians 12:14).

culture.title: The third heaven
culture.text: Jewish writings of the time described several levels of heaven.

culture.title: A thorn in the flesh
culture.text: Paul does not say what it was. Suggestions since early times include illness, poor eyesight (Galatians 4:15), or opponents.

2 Corinthians 13.audience: Paul warns of his third visit and closes with a blessing in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Ghost (2 Corinthians 13:14).

culture.title: Two or three witnesses
culture.text: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 19:15.

culture.title: An holy kiss
culture.text: A kiss was a common greeting among family and close friends.
